berakhot-6b-19-19.note: A man prayed behind the synagogue without turning to face it. Elijah the Prophet passed by and saw him, appearing to him as an Arab. He said to him: is this how you stand before your Master? Then he drew a sword and killed him.
berakhot-6b-19-19.why: Rav Huna has just said that one who prays behind the synagogue is called wicked, and Abaye limited this to someone who does not face the synagogue. The story shows how serious that offense is.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The biblical prophet, who in Talmudic stories returns to visit people, often in disguise.

terms.meaning: Praying outside the building facing away from it, so that he seems to turn his back on the congregation praying inside.

berakhot-7b-26-27.note: Rabbi Yitzhak asked Rav Nahman why he had not come to the synagogue to pray. Rav Nahman said he was too weak. Rabbi Yitzhak suggested he gather ten men at home to pray; Rav Nahman said that would be too much of a burden on them. Then let the congregation send a messenger to tell you when they are praying, Rabbi Yitzhak said, so you can pray at the same moment. When Rav Nahman asked why he was going to such lengths, Rabbi Yitzhak quoted Rabbi Yohanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai: the 'time of favor' in the Psalm is the time when the congregation prays.
berakhot-7b-26-27.why: The Gemara has been quoting Rabbi Yohanan's teachings in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai; this exchange introduces another of them, and other Sages then add their own verses showing the special power of praying with a community.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel who urges Rav Nahman to pray together with the congregation.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage and judge, here too weak to come to synagogue.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The leading Sage of the Land of Israel in the third century, quoted by Rabbi Yitzhak.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: A great second-century Sage, student of Rabbi Akiva, whose teaching Rabbi Yohanan passes on.

terms.meaning: A prayer quorum, called a minyan: the ten adult men needed for communal prayer.
A phrase from Psalms 69:14, read here as a moment when God is especially ready to accept prayer.

berakhot-16b-10-10.note: When Rabbi Eliezer's maidservant dies, his students come to comfort him as they would a mourner. He tries to avoid them, going upstairs, then into the gatehouse, then into the banquet hall, and they follow him each time. Finally he scolds them for missing the hint and reminds them of his own teaching: the formal mourning rites are not held for slaves. Instead one says to the owner what one says when an ox or donkey dies, 'May the Omnipresent replenish your loss.'
berakhot-16b-10-10.why: The mishna says Rabban Gamliel accepted condolences when his servant Tavi died, and the Gemara has just quoted a teaching that the mourning rites are not observed for slaves; this incident is the source of that teaching.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A leading Sage of the generation after the Temple's destruction, teacher of many students.

terms.meaning: After a burial, comforters lined up in rows and the mourners passed between them to receive words of comfort.
A special blessing recited in the mourners' presence, part of the formal rites of comforting them.
A name for God, literally 'the Place', used often in words of comfort.

berakhot-27b-14-21.note: A student asks Rabbi Yehoshua whether the evening prayer is optional or required and is told 'optional'; Rabban Gamliel, head of the Sages, tells him 'required'. Rabban Gamliel raises the question in the study hall, forces Rabbi Yehoshua to admit his view, and leaves him standing while he lectures. The angry assembly removes Rabban Gamliel and appoints the young Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, whose hair miraculously turns white. The study hall is opened to all students, and Rabban Gamliel keeps attending. Later he visits Rabbi Yehoshua, is shocked to learn he earns his living as a blacksmith, and begs forgiveness. Rabbi Yehoshua forgives him and goes with Rabbi Akiva to help restore him; the story's final arrangement is not given here.
berakhot-27b-14-21.why: The mishna says the evening prayer 'is not fixed', and the Gemara has just shown that the Sages disagreed whether it is optional or required; this is the famous dispute between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua on that very question.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Head (Nasi) of the Sages after the Temple's destruction, known for a firm, demanding leadership.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A leading Sage who holds the evening prayer is optional; poor, he works as a blacksmith.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: A wise, wealthy young Sage, a descendant of Ezra, chosen to replace Rabban Gamliel.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A great Sage from a family of converts; he backs Rabbi Yehoshua and then helps make peace.

people.name: Yehuda, the Ammonite convert
people.about: A convert who asks whether he may marry into the Jewish people.

terms.meaning: The president or head of the Sages and of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel.
A nickname for the Torah scholars, who 'battle' over the law in the study hall.
A tractate of the Mishna (the early collection of Jewish law) made up of testimonies about earlier rulings.
A priest who sprinkles purifying water and red-heifer ash on the impure; used here as an image for the rightful hereditary leader.

berakhot-30b-24-24.note: Mar, son of Ravina, held a wedding feast for his son and saw that the Sages there were getting too merry. He brought out a precious cup worth four hundred zuz and smashed it in front of them, and they grew sad.
berakhot-30b-24-24.why: The Gemara is discussing whether excessive joy is proper; it has just told of Sages rebuked for being too joyful, and follows this with Rav Ashi breaking a glass at his own son's wedding and a mournful song sung at Mar's feast.

people.name: Mar, son of Ravina
people.about: A Babylonian Sage who sobered his son's wedding guests by breaking an expensive cup.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; four hundred zuz was a very large sum.

berakhot-42a-4-4.note: Rav Pappa visited the home of Rav Huna, son of Rav Natan. After the meal was over, something more to eat was brought in, and Rav Pappa took it and ate without saying a new blessing. His hosts asked whether he did not hold that once a meal is finished one may not eat again without a blessing. He answered that the rule, correctly stated, speaks of the table being 'removed', not of the meal being finished.
berakhot-42a-4-4.why: The Gemara is working out when a meal counts as over, so that further food needs its own blessing; right after, Rava and Rabbi Zeira argue the same question at the Exilarch's house, using Rav Pappa's 'removed' wording.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Babylonian Sage and head of an academy, a visitor here.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Natan
people.about: A Babylonian Sage, the host of the meal.

terms.meaning: In Talmudic times each diner ate at a small table that was carried away when the meal ended. Taking it away, not just stopping eating, marks the meal's end.

berakhot-49a-21-21.note: Giddel bar Manyumi is standing near Rav Nahman when Rav Nahman forgets to add the special Shabbat passage to Grace after Meals. Rav Nahman goes back and says the whole Grace again from the beginning. Asked why, he cites Rav's teaching, as reported by Rabbi Sheila: one who made this mistake goes back to the beginning.
berakhot-49a-21-21.why: The Gemara has just reported Rav's ruling that one who forgot the Shabbat passage in Grace after Meals adds a short substitute blessing; this incident gives a conflicting report of Rav, which the discussion then reconciles.

people.name: Giddel bar Manyumi
people.about: A Sage who watches Rav Nahman and questions his practice.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage.

people.name: Rabbi Sheila
people.about: A Sage who reported Rav's ruling.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A founding Sage of Babylonian Talmudic learning, whose rulings are quoted throughout.

terms.meaning: The set of blessings said after eating bread. On Shabbat a special passage is added.

berakhot-60a-17-17.note: Yehuda bar Natan is walking behind Rav Hamnuna and lets out a sigh. Rav Hamnuna asks whether he wants to bring suffering on himself, quoting Job: 'that which I did fear is come upon me.' Yehuda replies with the verse 'Happy is the man who fears always,' and Rav Hamnuna answers that that verse is about fear of forgetting Torah.
berakhot-60a-17-17.why: The mishna calls a frightened prayer about a scream in the city a vain prayer, and the Gemara is praising trust over fear; this incident, like the one before it, teaches that one should fear only for one's Torah learning.

people.name: Yehuda bar Natan
people.about: A Sage, here walking with Rav Hamnuna.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A Babylonian Sage who rebukes his companion for sighing.
